utterances.text: And in spite of these positions that you mentioned here, the main source of your information as to the direction from which the bullet came was based on witness statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, it's only -- from what I got from the witness's statements, it's only the alleged shooting position, but I -- like, it's in the report. Sometimes I contradict the witness statements because I don't believe that the bullet might have originated from there. So it's largely from my own conclusions that I determine the point of origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a problem with this as I interpreted your report. We have an instance, for instance, where two eye-witnesses actually have contradictory statements as to where the bullet came from, and then, based on the statement of one of those eye-witnesses, you would go to a location where allegedly the bullet had come from, but you wouldn't go to the location where the other witness stated that the bullet came from there; correct? For instance, specifically speaking of the Jewish cemetery, a representative of the OTP said that one witness stated that the bullet had come from the Jewish cemetery, but you said that that was impossible because there were some buildings in between; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I said it would be -- for that incident, it was impossible because the buildings were in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you did not have occasion to see the crime report, the crime investigation, onsite investigation report, which would also establish or state where the bullet would have come from, and you did not rely on those as material facts or evidence that could help you form your conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I want to get back to a line I made earlier about the information that I received from the Prosecutor because I was asked yesterday during the proofing what information I had received and -- but because a lot of my material was in storage, I was not able to get to all my -- because it's on a CD-ROM, unfortunately, the CD-ROM in my laptop is -- the driver is broken, so I wasn't able to see all the information that I'd received. So there possibly are some witness reports that I've read, but still I didn't rely on the -- on the witness statements that much because I just wanted from my point of view what would be possible for a shooter to deliver a bullet on the incident side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that in your analysis, you relied specifically on what the Prosecutor told you about what a witness had told them. For instance, you said the infamous location of Grbavica. This information came from the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No. That is my own conclusion because Grbavica is featured in several descriptions of the incidents. So it was obviously, for the witnesses, a notorious location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now for a moment discuss the incident that you marked as incident 18. In the English version, that's on page 13; and in our instance in the indictment, it is P-12. Incident P-12, the wounding of Semsa Covrk. As a witness and a victim, she says that she had been hit from the direction of the airport. If you'd like to refresh your memory and take a look at the description of the incident. Do you remember that you handled this and processed this incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the victim says that the bullet came from the airport, and you provided your own arguments as to why you excluded the possibility of the bullet having come from the airport, and then you assessed that the bullet had come from a house that you marked, and you described the swathe of land from which -- an area from which the bullet would have come.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Like I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is, were you shown by a representative the OTP maps where -- from which you could see who was actually holding this location at the time? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The only location -- the only information about positions were that I knew the Sarajevo airport was under the control of UNPROFOR and from the brief description that she was facing VRS frontline positions at the Sarajevo, but I don't have knowledge of where exactly those positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, you do not know who controlled those positions that you said were the possible location where the bullet had come from; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is that I received the proofing notes from the Prosecutor, and based on them I realised that you did not actually read the indictment in the case of Dragomir Milosevic, and I'm pleased because this will provide for your impartiality and judgement. That is why I ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- I think my friend misspoke. The proofing note doesn't indicate he didn't read the indictment in the Milosevic matter. It indicated that he didn't read the judgement rendered by the court in the Milosevic matter. Just so it's clear. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said. I said judgement, and it's probably an interpretation error. I did refer to judgement. I apologise because it wouldn't be logical if it were an indictment, so I did use the word "judgement."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us discuss the next incident, incident number 8 in your report. That's on page 24 of the English version. In B/C/S, that's 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the incident marked in schedule B as incident number 8 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we've already touched upon this incident today. You determined as the site where the tram was hit an area between the museum and the university; is that correct? That is the same site that is mentioned in incident B-11 that you've shown us here today.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct. There were two incidents at the same site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please see Exhibit P491 that you've marked today. For both of these incidents, you drew as the site the area between the museum and the faculty - is that correct - claiming that on both these incidents, the tram had been hit through the tunnel from the Matalka building; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that the site where the tram was shown to have been hit, that you received the information as to the tram site from the Prosecution based on witness statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The problem that I have with this is that all the witnesses describing this incident mention that the tram had been hit near the barracks, and this is not only mentioned by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I disagree with that characterization of my friend. I don't know if this is an issue that should be discussed in the presence of the witness or what the practice here is, but I certainly don't agree that all of the witnesses indicate a different location in relation to incident B-8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my assertion is that this incident, as far as the witnesses are concerned, is described as the tram having been hit close to the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Your learned friend wants to suggest that maybe you discuss this in the absence of the witness. Are you able to indicate your attitude to that? I don't know what it is that is going to be discussed that requires the witness to be absent. You probably feel each other, know more or less which way you are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not see. I have no idea why there is any need for this witness to be absent. I'm not going to discuss here the witness statements. I just want to discuss the possible sites of the incident. I don't think it is necessary for the witness to leave the courtroom unless the Prosecutor is insisting or maybe wants to touch upon some other topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My only concern, of course, is that the witness is now going to be privy to information that he hasn't necessarily been privy to before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you insist on him being absent?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think that to preserve his potential evidence if he were ever asked about these incidents again in the future that he should be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These are some of the vicissitudes of trial that interrupt you in the middle of your testimony. I'm sorry to have to do this to you. Will you please excuse us for a short while. Don't go far. You will be called fairly soon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it matter if the witness's mike stays on? Doesn't matter. Okay. Who is starting?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll just indicate to the Court my concern. Thank you, Mr. Saxon. My friend has suggested to the witness that all of the witnesses agree that this incident took place in proximity to the Tito barracks. We've heard from one witness in relation to this incident so far. We have not yet heard from the other two witnesses who are scheduled to testify in relation to this matter. My respectful submission, it would not be a fair characterization of the two witnesses who have not yet testified to say that they are indicating a different location in proximity to the Tito barracks. Their anticipated evidence based on my review of their evidence is that in fact they will identify the same location that this witness has identified as the location for the tram when they indicate where they believe they were at the time it was hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me get clarity here. I understood Mr. Lukic - and Mr. Lukic, you can correct me if I'm wrong - to be talking about the witnesses on the basis of whose statements this witness worked, not any other witnesses that are going to be called by the Prosecution necessarily, but those witnesses that -- that provided information that he used.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are the same witnesses, Your Honour. So that's the difficulty, is that on the basis of the witness statements that we would hear about eventually viva voce, it's a mischaracterization, in my respectful submission, to say that they indicate a different location. To say that they all indicate it happened at the Tito barracks is not correct in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to simplify this completely, and I will rephrase my questions. But I think that based on the instructions that you issued, we can -- we can put a question to a witness regarding witness statements of witnesses that are yet to come and testify here. But to make this simpler, if you recall, there was a witness speaking about the shooting through the tunnel towards the direction of target "T," that he marked as "T," and the Prosecutor in his indictment with incident B-8, describing incident B-8, claims that the witness had been hit from the direction through this tunnel, and all I want to ask is whether -- I want to put it to this witness and ask whether it's possible to hit a target through the tunnel if the tram was in the vicinity of the barracks. That's all that I was aiming at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That question is completely different from saying all witnesses say A, B, C, number 1. Number 2, on the point of confronting a witness with the witness statement of witnesses yet to be called, yes, I accept that that is the guide-line, but there is some small procedure that you've got to follow before that, i.e., disclose to the Prosecution or the opposite member and the Bench who those witnesses are without revealing that to the witness on the stand. But if you are going -- if you just want to ask the question that you put now -- is it possible to shoot through the tunnel? What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Is it possible by shooting through the tunnel, that the witness indicated here, to hit a tram that was in the vicinity of the barracks? That's the only question I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that question would be perfectly legitimate without characterizing the statements of other witnesses. Thank you very much. If that is the case, shall we then call the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness then come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van Der Weijden, I will have this question for you: From the location that you indicated here was the Matalka building, it is possible through the tunnel that you marked to hit the tram if the tram was outside the Marshal Tito barracks at that moment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While we still have this map before us, let me ask you another thing. You marked with a "G" this rectangle here that you said was Grbavica. Do you know who controlled the area between the "G" area and the site where the tram was hit as seen in this picture? Which forces controlled this area during the incident, at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: So between the rectangle and the tram tracks? Well, I wasn't told, but I assume it's the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your understanding was that the Miljacka River was the natural frontline that actually divided the two forces, the BH Army and the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct, and that's why I assumed that north of the river is occupied by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion about this incident is that it was caused by automatic weapon fire. Could you tell us how you came to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The reason why I came to this conclusion, there is not mentioning of automatic fire by the witnesses, but for the incident it's easier for the machine-gun to be able to hit the tram than with a regular rifle because it is a moving target even though the line of sight -- the line of fire would be stationary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I read in your report. But if I were to tell you that the onsite investigation, the criminal investigation report indicates that only one bullet actually hit the tram, would that affect your conclusion in respect of the weapons used?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is your view that the tram could have been hit by several bullets that cannot be detected on the tram itself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, the problem with a machine-gun, a machine-gun isn't made to have all the bullets exactly at the same location if you fire the machine-gun. So if you fire a machine-gun, it's meant to give a spread of bullets to hit multiple targets so even though there's only one hit on the tram, there might be several hits above the tram going in buildings beyond the tram. It doesn't mean -- if there's only one hit, it doesn't mean it's semi-auto fire, semi-automatic fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the tram is in motion and if there is a trace that a bullet had hit the tram and this is material evidence, how can you then -- based on what can you conclude that the tram was hit by automatic weapons fire? Was this conclusion that you drew based on witness statements or what? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It was based on my conclusion that I thought it would be the most suitable weapon in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is based on your experience as a man who knows what type of weapon is best suited for a certain location. Your conclusion was that it's probable that an automatic weapon was used, or a machine-gun; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask but incident number 13 in your report. That's on page 27 of your report; B/C/S, that's on page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, this is incident B-10, and if I am correct, the OTP actually decided to exclude this incident. I think my colleague mentioned that they are not going to refer to this incident, and if I'm correct, then I will not refer to it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. This is the incident of 27 February 1995? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In conclusion, if I may, if this expert report is to be adopted as evidence, this item, this incident will not be part of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then move on to incident number 14 in your report. Your Honour, that's on page 30 of the English version, the hard copy of your report, and in the annex, Your Honour, in the schedule to the indictment, it's B-11.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, because we've already discussed this incident and you mentioned that you had analysed that document, so, Mr. Van Der Weijden, in footnote 5 in the B/C/S version, you mention ballistic evidence provided by Zlatko Medjodovic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I assume, then, that you read the ballistic report since you're referring to it; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I haven't because this was referred to in the situation. So it was included in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Your Honours. I don't see any footnotes in the English version, so I'm just having difficulty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a footnote 2 in the English version in the middle of page 30 of the hard copy, Azem Agovic, Alen Gicevic, and ballistic evidence from Zlatko Medjodovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in that ballistics report, once again we have the following situation, that the crime technicians just established one projectile, one bullet having hit the tram. Now, would that change your finding, and would you say that it wasn't a machine-gun after all, but an ordinary rifle, if I can put it that way, a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: There are also conclusions -- just a moment. I conclude that the machine-gun because she saw -- as I stated this, the -- Slavica Livnjak, the driver of tram 268 saw the tram ahead of her hit in the pantograph, and then heard a shot, so there were at least two projectiles separate from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I can conclude, then, that you arrived at that conclusion that it was indeed a machine-gun on the basis of a statement shown you by the witness and not on the basis of a crime report; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct because I have not read the crime report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now going to look at case number 10, and the English version of that is on page 43. It is, Your Honours, the incident in our annex B, number 9, and it refers to Spicaste Stijena or Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Who provided you with the information as to where the positions of the BH Army were located in that general locality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Partly, it is written down in the situation, and I was pointed out the location of Sharpstone by the investigator, and I was also told by the investigator that the Sharpstone and was occupied by the VRS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here towards the end of your analysis of this particular case, you say, since you established that it's a distance that is greater than 800 metres, the position from where the position was targeted, you said the distance from which they were hit was a great -- more than 800 metres, and without its sights, it's difficult to identify but nonetheless possible. Now, my question is, what can be seen with the naked eye at a distance of 800 metres if you are looking at a target which happens to be a human being? Can you actually see it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: With the naked eye, possibly you would see the optic moving, so you would see movement at 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And using sights with a 4-times magnification, can you see what the person is holding in their hands or carrying at a distance greater than 800 metres?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And the last incident that I'd like to refer to in your report is case number 3, and that is on page 43 of the English. No, I apologise. It's page 50. And it is annex 7 B of the indictment that we are dealing with now, that particular incident. It is (redacted) who was on the spot with her daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think, Your Honours, that we would have to go into private session for a moment because I seem to remember that one of those individuals was a protected witness, and I apologise if I've disclosed anything. I'm not quite sure, but I seem to remember that being the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we have a redaction at page 57, line 5, even though the stenographer didn't pick up the name, and may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you refreshed your memory as to that section of your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Take a moment.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as I understood your analysis and your conclusions with relation to this specific incident is that the location which was indicated by the witness shows it to be at a distance over 1.200 metres so that it was impossible for the sniper to target in the way in which the witness described it. That is your first conclusion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then on the basis of your assessments of the situation and the given locality, you go on to reconstruct the incident on the basis of which you consider that the sniper should have entered -- must have entered no-man's land and then targeted that way as described further on by the witness.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, you cannot tell us, nor do you know, nor can you assume, whether it was a VRS or BH Army sniper who was there on that no-man's land? You can't say either way, can you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It would be very difficult. The only thing that I would be able to get from the facts and from the terrain is that the sniper would have come from the direction of the VRS because the ABiH positions that I was -- that I was shown were up on a ridge, and it would be very difficult to get down from the ridge to a position, and it would be almost impossible to get up to the ridge to get back again to their own troops. So it would be very dangerous for them to do that. So that's why I concluded that the shooter must have come from the east because it's into a valley which offers some cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is based on what the investigator of the OTP told you was no man's land, that particular territory, so that's how you made your conclusions; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: He told me that that had been no-man's land at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because the Trial Chamber in the Dragomir Milosevic trial in paragraph 406 of the judgement was not able to arrive at a conclusion as to who could have arrived at that locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't think it's appropriate -- my friend congratulated the witness earlier for the fact that he hasn't read the judgement, and it's not appropriate, in my respectful submission, to be making any reference to the findings of another trial Tribunal. This Chamber is going to make its own assessment of the facts and make its own findings based on evidence that it hears, which may differ from the evidence that was heard in some respects in D. Milosevic. SO there ought not be any questioning, in my respectful submission, of the witness based on a judgement, A, he's never read, and, B, that this Tribunal ought not to be taking into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be allowed to comment. I don't wish in any way to suggest what the conclusions of the Trial Chamber might be. I'm just putting a theoretical question to the witness, and my theoretical question was that you can't really know who was on that no man's land, who could have reached that piece of no man's land. So I don't see why I can't put that to the witness and ask him something that came from anybody's conclusion, regardless of the fact whether it was another Trial Chamber or an article in the newspaper, to be quite frank. I think it's an assumption. I allow the witness to look at an assumption, especially as he is an expert witness, so why can't I put somebody else's conclusion to this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The trouble is the conclusion that you are putting is a Trial Chamber's conclusion. It's not a conclusion reached by another witness. Now, I'm not quite sure whether you want this Trial Chamber to take the findings of another Trial Chamber as testimony. So there is absolutely nothing wrong in putting an assumption to the witness. There's everything wrong in putting a legal finding of another Trial Chamber to the witness. He is not -- he's a layperson in law, for starters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did not wish to put this as a legal conclusion, Your Honours, but as a conclusion of fact, as a fact-finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but that's still a conclusion of the Trial Chamber. It's not a statement of a witness. Now, this Trial Chamber is going to make its conclusions based on the evidence it hears. Do you want the factual finding of another trial to be part of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to do is this: Through my question, I'm not asking for a factual conclusion to be adopted, but I want the witness to take a position, his own position with respect to a statement of fact, whether that statement of fact has been made by a court of law, a Trial Chamber, or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be perhaps be helpful if you put up the factual assumption to the witness without characterising the assumption as a finding of another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, the representative of the OTP indicated the location where -- and he told you what was no man's lands, what the area under the VRS control was, and what the area under ABiH control was. Now, in this specific case, you drew your conclusions on the basis of your own experience from which place it would be best -- well, that's a sort of unfortunate expression, but it would be most suitable to hit the target as described; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I concluded what would be a suitable shooting position, a tactically good shooting position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right. So in analysing this section, you did not have any documents available or facts or evidence available indicating who could have shot from where, that is to say, the "who" being which member of any army, the member of either one of the armies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just take a moment, Your Honours, to consult my colleague because I'm reaching the end of my cross-examination, to see if I haven't left anything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I finish with my cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Van Der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic. Any re-examination, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Very brief. I better begin by asking if the report could be marked as an exhibit at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P490 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 493 marked for identification -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it marked for identification? What is the reason for that? Did I hear you say marked for identification, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's what I heard, Your Honours. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking it be marked for identification. I'm just asking it be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I thought I heard.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So it will be Exhibit P493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you wanted to say something just before the re-examination begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say this: According to earlier practice with respect to expert reports that I can state my opinion, that is to say whether I consider that it should be admitted or not, whether it should be admitted or not, so specifically linked to the expert report, we usually did this at the end, right at the end, after redirect and when the expert witness leaves the courtroom that then we can give our arguments. So I think that this may be premature. It's premature to do this at this point about the admission of the expert report now. I feel it's premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, I'll not ask the question. What do you want to do? Do you have any response to that, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands in terms of the practice here. If my friend has an argument he wants to make about the -- whether the report should be marked as an exhibit and he wishes to wait until I've asked my two questions in redirect, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll hold the allocation of an exhibit number to the end of your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just two questions for you, Mr. Van Der Weijden. My friend was asking a question about the ability at a distance of 800 metres or greater to see what a human being was holding in their hand with -- he indicated with sights equipped with 4-times magnification, and your response was that it would be very difficult. In those circumstances, if you can't tell what the person is holding, are you entitled, for example, to assume it's a weapon?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would not be entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And my other question relates to, there were two incidents that my friend asked you about where he indicated that there was only one bullet -- I guess evidence of only one bullet found on examination of the trams, and just for clarification, can one bullet injure more than one person?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, it would be almost impossible if it were to happen out in the open apart from people being behind each other; then the bullet could penetrate one person and then penetrate again in the other person. But bullets tend to start to fragment on hitting hard material, so if we would take a tram which has probably aluminium side walls and glass windows, glass strips, the copper casing of the lead core of the bullet causing it to fragment into two or more bigger parts, which could both injure people, so it could be one bullet that causes more wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Those are all of my questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear nothing through the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I -- because I do understand some French, I think I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'd -- completely ignoramus, some of us, so we must understand the question before we can let you answer. French/English booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's fine now, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you interpret for us now, or do you want the Judge to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, could the Judge repeat the question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was this. It concerns the incidents on the tram. Now, is it possible in your opinion with respect to the positions of the snipers, was it possible to establish whether they were able to distinguish between civilian and military persons in the tram, for example?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it would not be, and I would like to explain that. Trams, they have glass windows. If they're dirty, it can already at 50 metres to be very difficult to look into the tram, so even from a larger distance it would be more difficult, and trams, they wobble a bit; they don't have the suspension of cars, so then the people inside, they always -- they are always moving, and then even further is -- if the windows were to be cleaner, they would reflect light, so it would be very difficult to look inside a tram. I think from 300 metres it would almost be impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Reflect light assuming that the light comes from the side where the sniper is?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Not necessarily so. It would be like these glass windows here in the courtroom, that you can see your own reflection in the window, so making it more difficult to see what's behind the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: None for me, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, sir. Thank you so much for taking the time off to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down and travel well back home. I hope it's not far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I still wish to have the report tendered as an exhibit. I'm not certain as to what the basis for my friend's objection is, so perhaps we could hear from him, and I could respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll find out. That report has been tendered. Mr. Lukic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to put forward our arguments with respect to this expert report. Bearing in mind what we've just heard and what we have read, the Defence agrees, yes, yes, yes. Just that. The Defence considers that parts of the expert report in points 3 and 4 are not contentious as far as we are concerned and that they will be useful to the Trial Chamber. However, the Defence considers that the methodology used by this expert in this report referring to points 1, 2, and 5 as such, that it cannot be useful to the Trial Chamber in light of his explanations as to how he analysed some of the incidents. I don't want to go into that at any length and to repeat the answers that we received from him, but he made his expert report on the basis of some assumptions, locations provided to him by a representative of the OTP without taking into consideration, in my opinion, relative material evidence which was also accessible to him. So I think it is only with a complete analysis of the overall evidence would he be able to come up with something that could be helpful for the Trial Chamber in their deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think if I remember to turn on the button, that would be helpful. I think if I understand my friend's argument, it is that there is additional information that could have been made available to him that was not available to him or was not reviewed by him that may have affected his opinions. First, it was open to my friend as he did in some extent in cross-examination to put that additional material to him and to see if it altered his opinion, so he's had that opportunity. And secondly, any issues with respect to deficiencies in his methodology would ultimately go to the weight to be accorded his report and not its admissibility. The test for admissibility would be, is he an expert? This Chamber has already found that he is an expert. Does the subject matter of the report fall within that area of expertise? Again, that's already been ruled on by this Chamber, and any other issues, in my respectful submission, go to weight only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The report is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. 493, P493?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's Exhibit P493, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling the next witness, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am not. I was going to ask permission to be excused, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon. Yes, you are right. Mr. Saxon, you want to do that later?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For once, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you always are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I doubt that. Perhaps it would be time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Cannata will call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Poje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: My name is Jozef Poje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 4892 on the e-court, and actually, page 4 of the English copy and 6 of the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to briefly review your professional background, and I see that you have a copy of some document in front of you, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: What is that document, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: This is a document that I prepared while I was an expert witness in the case of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, sir, from time to time you might need to refresh your memory. If you wish to do so, please ask the Court's permission. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: It's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you graduated from the JNA military academy in Zadar in 1971; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly tell the Court what positions and ranks you had with the JNA after you graduated in 1971?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: After I graduated the military academy in Zadar, for four years I was a commander of a mortar battery of a mixed artillery division. Between 1975 and 1978, I commanded an anti-armour battery of 100 millimetre in Ptuj. In 1978, I was transferred to the artillery school centre in Zadar where I worked as a lecturer in theory and rules of firing. I stayed in Zadar for 13 years. I was a lecturer in firing theory and artillery firing rules, including a year at the school for reserve officers, ten years at the military academy, and two years, I taught a course for artillery battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might attempt to be of some assistance - I don't know if this is or not - to the Prosecution, with regard to this gentleman's qualifications as an expert as it relates to artillery, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: That's very much of assistance. We appreciate Mr. Guy-Smith's remarks, and now we can move on to a different topic of my examination. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, did you testify as an expert on artillery issues before this Tribunal on two occasions, the Strugar case in 2004 and the Martic case in 2006?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. I testified as an expert witness in both those cases, General Strugar and Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. And in case of the Prosecutor versus Martic, were you asked by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal to prepare an expert report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. I was given a task to prepare a report as an artillery expert in the case of Mr. Martic, and I prepared a written report which I submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Madam Registrar, can we please go back to page 1 of the document in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the report that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: It's a report for the Martic case that you prepared and signed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, in the Martic case, what were you asked to address in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In the Martic case, there were two focal tasks that I had, two main tasks. The first was, where was the multiple rocket-launcher Orkan, where its location was; and secondly, to provide expert testimony on the dispersion of projectiles in the course of a firing of that weapon, and in relation to dispersion that I mentioned, there was generally a question of whether such a rocket attack was permissible when a settlement or a settled area was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. For clarity of the record, when you say: "... whether such a rocket attack ..." do you mean by that the shelling of Zagreb on 2nd and 3rd May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what the case was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, moving to the sources of your report, can you tell the Court, what kinds of sources have you used and reviewed to prepare your report for the Martic case?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In preparing the report, I used relatively large number of works on the -- that I used in the report itself; and as for the two main issues that I discussed that I've already mentioned so far, one of them being where the Orkan weapon was located and the second issue being the shelling of Zagreb itself, I used the directive on the use or employment of the Serbian army of Krajina as a source; and secondly, I also used the document, the preparation and analysis of combat readiness of the units of the Serbian army of Krajina from 1995; and the third document was the raising of combat readiness of the 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Let me stop you here for a moment. Apart from these three documents that you just have mentioned, can I take you to page 3 of the English copy of the report, which will be page 4 of the B/C/S one. Thank you. Now, do you see in front of you a list of documents?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Is that the list of documents that you have reviewed to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the complete or full list of documents that I used in preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, would you be able to briefly talk the Court through the methodology that you used to prepare the Martic report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Concerning the main question in the report, the main issue, which was who decided on the use of a multiple rocket-launcher Orkan, as I've already mentioned, I used the literature mentioned earlier from which we can see the following: First --

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Please hold on. Now, the question -- my question has a more general attitude. I would like you to speak -- I would like you to explain to the Court, what was the methodology that you have generally used throughout the whole report that you have drafted, not just one issue, but the whole report. Roughly, what methodology you have used to prepare that report, apart from specific issues. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear. I studied thoroughly the literature that was provided to me from the Office of the Prosecutor and also the literature that I found myself, and I tried to answer the questions that were put by the Office of the Prosecutor, and if we look at the contents of the report, we can see that it moves from the general use of artillery and the general rules of firing through an analysis of the types of firing, the methods of firing, types of preparation for firings, dispersion of projectiles, and finally, to the report itself on the issue that concerned Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, let's move on to the substance of your report. We don't have time today to review each single information that you have detailed in your report. What I would propose is to guide you through each section of the report. Can we start from the first substantive section, which is section number 3 which can be found at -- one second, Your Honour. Page 6 of the English copy. I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S page for that document. Now, sir, the section number 3 is entitled "technical aspects of artillery." Now, can you briefly describe to the Court what it is that you address in this section of the report.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In this section, I discuss the technical aspects of artillery, and I discuss fire support, classification of artillery, the types -- definition and types of artillery firings, definition and types of targets and artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, sir, as I already said, we don't have time to go into details, but can I ask to you please have a look at page 37 of the English copy, which will be page 45 of your B/C/S version, and I would like you to briefly discuss the characteristics of the M-87 Orkan multiple rocket-launcher. Now, before you start, could you please tell the Court what an M-87 Orkan multiple rocket-launcher is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, if it's of any assistance to the Prosecution, the Defence has no objection to the information that's contained with regard to those pages of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I can move on to another topic which I think will be a little bit more difficult for the Defence to agree on, which will be 55 of the English report, page 64 of the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, in section 392 of your report, you discussed the issue of command and control with regard to artillery. Can you briefly describe to the Court what is that your report says about the issue of command and control over artillery pieces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Well, I discuss here the command of artillery, and that it is the job of the commander of joint tactical and operational units, commanders, and commands of artillery units in the process of preparation and conduct and carrying out of combat tasks and other tasks. Also, I stressed that the artillery is commanded by a joint tactical and operational unit directly or through his chief of artillery. The use of artillery is the sole responsibility of the commander of the joint tactical and operational group, unit. The artillery is commanded by the command -- by the commander of the supported unit of any level. That would be the gist of command and control of artillery unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 4913, please. Can we move on to page 11 of the English copy and 6 of the B/C/S. Can we please have -- I'm waiting for page 11 of the English copy, please. Thank you. Can we please have paragraph 4.2 zoomed in, which would be the first item on the English copy in front of you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Is that a document that you used to prepare your section 392 of your report where you discuss command and control over the Orkan units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document that I relied on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, sir, what does this document say about command and control with the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether the question calls for anything more than just the witness reading that which is said, unless you're asking for -- unless the gentleman is asking for an interpretation. The manner in which the question is put is a bit vague, but I leave it in his fine hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm simply asking the witness to report his conclusions on this document and the way he treated the information in this report -- in this document to compile his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Could you please answer to my question. Do you remember that, or would you like me to re-ask the question?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I will. Now, what is it in this document that you have used to draft your section of your report on command and control over the M-87 Orkan units with the SVK?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I suppose that you mean the document raising or increasing combat readiness, the order issued by RKS GSVK of the 1st of May, 1995, number 209.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you to concentrate your attention on the document that you have in front of you. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Well, I can see in front of me two documents. One of them is in the English language, and the other one is in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, this is the very reason that I rose before. Perhaps if we could have the specific language, and I have no objection to that, which I believe is 4, section number 2, read to the witness, and after that -- the witness has that information, he can perhaps comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or the witness can read that language himself and tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness, can you please read out the language at paragraph 4.2 in the B/C/S document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat which item you are referring to, and which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, you have a screen in front of you. Please disregard the paper copy that you have in front of you. All right. Follow me. You have a screen in front of you. You have a screen in front of you, sir. Could you please look at the document in front of you, the B/C/S document. Do you see that? Do you see a chapter number 4 of that document in the screen in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph number 2 of that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it says the following in that item: "Unit Orkan is a part of the formation of the 9th Artillery Regiment, and its utilization shall be approved exclusively by the commander of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: That's not what my English translation says, Your Honour. Can I ask you for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, you have the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thanks. It is my entire fault, Your Honour. I called up the wrong 65 ter number. It is clear now. So can I actually have 65 ter 476 on the screen, please. Can we please move to page 11 of the English copy and 10 of the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, can you read out paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: It's one page after this one in the B/C/S, sorry, page 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: One next page, please. Thank you. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a document, the directive on the employment of the Serbian Krajina Army from February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you review this document to prepare the report for the Martic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I did review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: What information did you take out of this document to prepare for your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In preparing my report, I used item 5.8 under number 2, paragraph 2. The artillery group of VBR Main Staff of Orkan, and then it says the group commander is the weapons commander, SLR 262 millimetre, firing position in the general Korenica sector, and the tasks that were assigned to this artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, can you help us with the acronyms. Let's start with VBR. What is VBR?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: AG is artillery group; VBR is multiple rocket-launcher; GS is Main Staff; and then in parenthesis, Orkan, which is the name of the multiple rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The following are the commander of the self-propelled weapon, 262 millimetre. It's the same weapon, Orkan multiple rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Can I have this document admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are we admitting that page or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: The entire document, which is the one that the expert witness Poje used to prepare his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, can I take you back to your report, please. Can we have it back on the screen. It's 4892. Can we move to page 58 of the English version. Can I have it in B/C/S as well. Thank you. Page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, this is section 4 of your report entitled "Doctrine of Using Fire Support." Can you briefly describe to the Court what it is that you address in this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In this part of my report, in this chapter, "Doctrine of Using Fire Support," I talk about the planning of artillery firings, the use of the artillery as such, the target selection, and they are the three main contents of that chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have any time to go any deeper to that, so I'll move on to section 5, which can be found at page 60 of the English report, 71 of the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, this is section 5 of your report entitled "Use of Artillery Support in Populated Areas." Can you briefly describe to the Court what it is discussed in this section, please?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In that respect and in that chapter, we look at what effects the artillery and it going into operation in populated areas, the problems that arise when you shoot targets in a populated area. I talk about artillery preparation, the choice of weapons and targets, as well, for firing in populated areas. That for the most part would be the contents of that particular chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can I take you to section 5.1. It's page 60, where we are right now. Now, I'm going to read to you the last paragraph of this section, of section 5.1, and I quote: "The Serbian Krajina army units did not conduct an attack on the city of Zagreb. This means that the M-87 Orkan SRL squad had no need to conduct direct support operations but was conducting general support operations, most probably to terrorise and fire on the population, their property, and their infrastructure." Firstly, can you please tell the Court what the, again, acronym SRL stand for, if you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Self-propelled -- the SRL is self-propelled rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to explain the statement that I've just read out to you to the Court. Perhaps we can start by explaining, what is the difference, could you describe, between a direct support operation as opposed to a general support operation. Can you tell the Court about that division?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Direct support is the action of the artillery on targets which have direct effects on the course of the activity of that particular unit, the unit carrying out the operation. For example, direct support to a brigade, the brigade artillery targets the enemy with the aim of carrying out the tasks and assignments of the brigade itself. That means artillery action for the needs of a concrete specific assignment while general support, generally artillery fire support is the fire action of supporting artillery but on targets which do not affect the activity of the supported unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, what kind of support operation was that carried out in Zagreb on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that there was no attack on the city of Zagreb itself but only artillery action - in this case, the action of Orkan - to my mind, this was general support.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, can you now explain what do you mean when you say that there was no attack on the city of Zagreb itself, whereas you discussed the shelling through Orkan rockets against the same city? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we look at the documents, the city of Zagreb itself was not attacked by units of the Serbian Army of Krajina. The target of the attack was not Zagreb, and units were not sent to attack the city of Zagreb. In actual fact, they were at a great distance from Zagreb, and for some reason, possibly because there was thought in advance when special targeting was done on military facilities in the town of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: When you say that the city of Zagreb itself was not attacked by units of the Serbian Army of Krajina, you mean ground troops and aviation troops, that sort of troops?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I mean the action of the army as a whole. As far as I know, it wasn't attacked by armoured infantry units. They didn't attack the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, what do you base upon your proposition that the use of Orkans against the city of Zagreb was carried out, and I quote: "... most probably to terrorise and fire on the population, their property, and infrastructure." What is the basis of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: If we look at the errors in initial elements and the preparation thereof, and if we look at the dispersion of the targets when multiple-barrel launchers are used - in this particular case, it was the Orkan SRL - then we come to the conclusion on the basis of the firing tables that the image of dispersion was very great; and if a mean hit went through the centre of the military target - let us assume that because I don't have the necessary information as to what the military target was of the shooting - so if we take the mean value, targeting the centre of a military target, then the surface of dispersion, the area dispersion is very great, which automatically means that part of the hits will fall outside and away from the target itself and inflict losses on the population, the infrastructure, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, I'm running a little bit late. Can I have some extra time? I promise I'll keep it within ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, can we please move to page 61 of the English copy of your report, which is section 6, which can be found at page 73 of the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, this is section 6 of your report, which is entitled: "The Use of VBR By the SVK on 2 and 3 May." In this section, you analyse three documents. We already reviewed the first one, which is 65 ter 476, which has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can I please now have 65 ter 4913. We've been there before. This is the document that we've shown to the witness a little bit earlier. Can I have page 11 of the English and 6 of the B/C/S original and have paragraph 4.2 zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, did you use this document to compile section 6 of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document that speaks about preparation analysing the combat readiness of the artillery, and I used .4, the task to be realised in 1985, and subsection 2: The Orkan unit is within the 7th MAP, and its utilisation shall be approved exclusively by the commander of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: So what did you take from this document that is significant to the section of your report dealing with command and control of Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: From this document, you can see where Orkan was located at that point in time, and what is even more important, perhaps, is the section which says that its deployment is exclusively approved by the commander, the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina. So it is under the direct command of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Can I have this document admitted into evidence, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We may do that. May I just find out, what does the acronym MAP stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mixed artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, can we move to 65 ter 4888.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document in front of you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents that you used to prepare section 6 of your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is one of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is important, what is significant to your report in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: In this -- this document is about raising combat readiness and talks about the transfer of Orkan from the present positions to a new location, so the relocation of Orkan, and that new location is at the command post of the 21st Corps. I think what is interesting to note here and look at is paragraph 4, which says that the commander of the Orkan squad is hereby deployed to the 21st corps command post in readiness for the reception of tasks from the commander of the SVK or Colonel Dilas, so it says that Orkan is under the direct command of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina and its commander or Colonel Dilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: The document was signed by General-Lieutenant Celeketic, Lieutenant-General Celeketic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you know what position General Celeketic had at this time in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I think that at the time, he was the command of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we move this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is received into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the basis of these documents that you have just looked at, is whether your own military experience, your own expertise as an artillery expert, what conclusion did you reach as to who commanded and controlled the M-87 Orkans which were fired upon Zagreb on May 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents that I looked at, and we've mentioned three of those here, we can say that the tasks and assignments given to Orkan were issued by the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina or, rather, its commander or Colonel Dilas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have just one more question, Your Honour. Then I'm done with this witness. Can we move to page 67 of the English report, which is 4892, and page 80 of the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Sir, section 6.3 contains your conclusions of the report. Would you briefly describe your conclusions to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: On the basis of everything that I have become aware of, on the basis of the literature that I studied and the documents that I was shown or had access to, I concluded that even if there were military targets in the city of Zagreb, due to the city's population density and its characteristics, the use of using rockets for targets had no sense because in targeting those facilities, this would have an effect on the population, its infrastructure, and all the rest. So once again, let me say that I consider that there was absolutely no sense in targeting Zagreb because it was known that there would be a lot of casualties among the civilians, that it was completely unreasonable, therefore, to target Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour, and I'm grateful of the extra time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You know General Perisic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you worked with him at the artillery centre in Zagreb, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was first chief of the department for tactics, and after, head of the artillery school centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to approach the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had a hard choice to make, I believe. That was in June of 1991 when there was the emerging war with Slovenia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And among other things, you sought General Perisic's counsel concerning how best for you to proceed, and by that, I mean whether or not to remain in the then JNA or - because you were Slovenian - to terminate your service with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: I don't see a question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm waiting for -- okay, my question to you is, you asked General Perisic's counsel, and by that I mean his views, on the issue of whether you should remain in the JNA or terminate your service with the JNA because you were Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, 1991, I tabled a request to leave the Yugoslav People's Army and stated the reasons I wished to do that. The head of the artillery school centre, General Perisic, who was Colonel Perisic at the time, called me to come to his office. He asked me whether I had my mind set on leaving the army and when I said, yes, I had made up my mind, he asked me whether I had a job to go to in Slovenia, and when I answered in the affirmative, he wished me well, bon voyage, and gave his subordinates the task of doing everything to see that I could leave the Yugoslav People's Army the very next day, on the 2nd. So I'm very grateful to him for having done that, and whenever I talk to anybody about how I came to leave the Yugoslav People's Army, I always speak of General Perisic in the best of terms because I had absolutely no problems in leaving the Yugoslav People's Army, nor did anybody attempt to hold me back, and as I had made up my mind, he respected my decision and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. I'd like to talk to you for a moment about your report, and very briefly, you first prepared this report for another case; correct? For the Martic case?
